title: I taught Ephraim to walk (Hosea 11:1–4)
hook: God as a parent holding a toddler's hands, bending down to feed

segments.voice: Yesterday, the lions' den: Daniel kept praying at his open window three times a day, law or no law. Your line was the window stays open. Did you keep one small appointment with what matters? Day four hundred eighty-two.

Watch a parent teach a toddler to walk. They crouch behind the child, one finger in each tiny fist, and shuffle forward bent nearly double. Their back aches. The child has no idea anyone is holding on. The child thinks they are walking all by themselves, and that's the point. Later, at the table, the same parent leans down with a spoon, patient, while half of it ends up on the floor. Most of us were held like that once, and none of us remember it. Around seven hundred years before Jesus, a prophet named Hosea reached for exactly this picture to describe God. Not a king on a throne. A parent on their knees in the hallway.

Hosea preached in the northern kingdom of Israel, and in his book the north is often called Ephraim, after its largest tribe. Chapter eleven opens like a family album. In the King James Bible: "When Israel was a child, then I loved him, and called my son out of Egypt." The Exodus, remembered not as a battle but as a parent calling a child home. Then the toddler scene: "I taught Ephraim also to go, taking them by their arms; but they knew not that I healed them." That's the ache in the chapter. The child was held, fed and healed, and never noticed. Verse four keeps going: "I drew them with cords of a man, with bands of love." Not chains for an animal. Human cords, the kind a person uses to guide someone they love. And then a farmer's picture: God as the one who lifts the yoke off the ox's jaw and bends down to feed it. The chapter isn't sweet all the way through. Hosea also names the people's turning away, and the hard years coming. But a few verses later God says, in effect, my heart is turned within me; I can't give you up. The love outlasts the anger. Matthew's Gospel later borrows the first line, out of Egypt have I called my son, and hears it in the story of the young Jesus coming back from Egypt. Christians often read Hosea that way, on two levels at once: Israel's story, and a pattern that Jesus walks again. Either way, the picture stays. God, in this book, is the one on their knees.

segments.voice: Here's the practice: care for a small one. Settle, and breathe. First, remember. Bring to mind someone who held you up before you could stand: a parent, a grandparent, an older cousin, a teacher. You may not remember the moment. Hosea's point is that you probably wouldn't. Just picture their hands. Then think of a small one in your life now: a child, a pet, a seedling on the windowsill, a younger colleague finding their feet. Choose one small act of care you can give them today. If you pray, you can give thanks for the hands that held you. If you don't, simply let the gratitude sit. The bell holds the time.
I taught Ephraim to walk. Hosea's picture of God as a parent bent over a toddler, holding their arms, feeding them, healing them unseen.

howItsDone: Many Christians read Hosea 11 as one of the tenderest pictures of God in the Bible, and preachers often pair it with the parable of the prodigal son; Matthew 2:15 quotes its first verse in the story of Jesus' childhood.

original.note: Hebrew: love. Hosea's "bands of love" are literally cords of ahavah.

trapdoor: what you thought: an old line about a tribe learning to walk.
what it means: God pictured as a parent bent over a toddler, holding their arms, feeding them, healing them while they never noticed.
what a scholar hears: Ephraim stands for the northern kingdom of Israel, and Matthew 2:15 reads the chapter's first verse again in the story of Jesus.

notes: The index word/title says 'to walk'; the KJV reads 'to go'. The script explains this. Consider whether the title should stay modern.
Dating Hosea to roughly 700 years before Jesus (he prophesied in the 8th century BC, before the fall of Samaria in 722 BC). Confirm the phrasing.
Verse 4's yoke/feeding picture is paraphrased; translations differ on whether the image is an infant lifted to the cheek or an ox's yoke. The KJV supports the yoke reading. Confirm.
Hosea 11:8 ('mine heart is turned within me') is paraphrased, not quoted. Confirm 'how can I give you up' paraphrase is fair.
Typological reading of Matthew 2:15 described as common among Christians, not ranked against other readings.
